verses.text: When Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see, he called Esau his elder son, and said to him, “My son?” He said to him, “Here I am.”
He said, “See now, I am old. I don’t know the day of my death.
Now therefore, please take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field, and take me venison.
Make me savory food, such as I love, and bring it to me, that I may eat, and that my soul may bless you before I die.”
Rebekah heard when Isaac spoke to Esau his son. Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it.
Rebekah spoke to Jacob her son, saying, “Behold, I heard your father speak to Esau your brother, saying,
‘Bring me venison, and make me savory food, that I may eat, and bless you before Yahweh before my death.’
Now therefore, my son, obey my voice according to that which I command you.
Go now to the flock, and get me from there two good young goats. I will make them savory food for your father, such as he loves.
You shall bring it to your father, that he may eat, so that he may bless you before his death.”
Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, “Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.
What if my father touches me? I will seem to him as a deceiver, and I would bring a curse on myself, and not a blessing.”
His mother said to him, “Let your curse be on me, my son. Only obey my voice, and go get them for me.”
He went, and got them, and brought them to his mother. His mother made savory food, such as his father loved.
Rebekah took the good clothes of Esau, her elder son, which were with her in the house, and put them on Jacob, her younger son.
She put the skins of the young goats on his hands, and on the smooth of his neck.
She gave the savory food and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob.
He came to his father, and said, “My father?” He said, “Here I am. Who are you, my son?”
Jacob said to his father, “I am Esau your firstborn. I have done what you asked me to do. Please arise, sit and eat of my venison, that your soul may bless me.”
Isaac said to his son, “How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?” He said, “Because Yahweh your God gave me success.”
Isaac said to Jacob, “Please come near, that I may feel you, my son, whether you are really my son Esau or not.”
Jacob went near to Isaac his father. He felt him, and said, “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.”
He didn’t recognize him, because his hands were hairy, like his brother, Esau’s hands. So he blessed him.
He said, “Are you really my son Esau?” He said, “I am.”
He said, “Bring it near to me, and I will eat of my son’s venison, that my soul may bless you.” He brought it near to him, and he ate. He brought him wine, and he drank.
His father Isaac said to him, “Come near now, and kiss me, my son.”
He came near, and kissed him. He smelled the smell of his clothing, and blessed him, and said, “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which Yahweh has blessed.
God give you of the dew of the sky, of the fatness of the earth, and plenty of grain and new wine.
Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers. Let your mother’s sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you. Blessed be everyone who blesses you.”
As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had just gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting.
He also made savory food, and brought it to his father. He said to his father, “Let my father arise, and eat of his son’s venison, that your soul may bless me.”
Isaac his father said to him, “Who are you?” He said, “I am your son, your firstborn, Esau.”
Isaac trembled violently, and said, “Who, then, is he who has taken venison, and brought it me, and I have eaten of all before you came, and have blessed him? Yes, he will be blessed.”
When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried with an exceeding great and bitter cry, and said to his father, “Bless me, even me also, my father.”
He said, “Your brother came with deceit, and has taken away your blessing.”

He said, “Isn’t he rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times. He took away my birthright. See, now he has taken away my blessing.” He said, “Haven’t you reserved a blessing for me?”
Isaac answered Esau, “Behold, I have made him your lord, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants. I have sustained him with grain and new wine. What then will I do for you, my son?”
Esau said to his father, “Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, my father.” Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.
Isaac his father answered him, “Behold, of the fatness of the earth will be your dwelling, and of the dew of the sky from above.
By your sword will you live, and you will serve your brother. It will happen, when you will break loose, that you shall shake his yoke from off your neck.”
Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father blessed him. Esau said in his heart, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand. Then I will kill my brother Jacob.”
The words of Esau, her elder son, were told to Rebekah. She sent and called Jacob, her younger son, and said to him, “Behold, your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you.
Now therefore, my son, obey my voice. Arise, flee to Laban, my brother, in Haran.
Stay with him a few days, until your brother’s fury turns away;
until your brother’s anger turn away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send, and get you from there. Why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?”

Rebekah said to Isaac, “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these, of the daughters of the land, what good will my life do me?”

footnotes.content: Isaac is old and his eyes have grown dim, so he calls for Esau to receive his blessing. There is something quietly poignant about a father longing to bless his son one last time, not knowing how blind he truly is to what is happening in his own house. How often we try to do the right thing while missing the greater work God is doing behind the scenes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac says he does not know the day of his death, and so he wants to bless Esau before that day comes. We all live with that same uncertainty, though we may not say it aloud. I find it humbling to remember that our lives are in the Lord's hands, and the only lasting blessing is the one He gives to those who trust in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac sends Esau out to hunt with bow and quiver, as he had always done. There is tenderness here - a father delighting in the son he loves, giving him one last chance to serve him in the way they have always shared. Even in our fading strength, we long to love and bless those God has given us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac wants savory food made, so that his soul may bless Esau before he dies. The language is beautiful - blessing flows from a heart full of love and satisfaction. Our God, unlike Isaac, never blesses by accident or in partial blindness; He blesses fully and freely those He has chosen in Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah hears Isaac speak to Esau, and immediately her ears are open. A household that has loved different sons is about to unravel in full view. I grieve how favoritism plants seeds of strife, and how quickly hidden plans begin to grow when love has grown partial.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah speaks privately to Jacob, not to Isaac. She moves in secret, though the God who gave the oracle of Genesis 25:23 had already said the older would serve the younger. The tragedy here is not that the younger receives the blessing, but that both mother and son grasp at God's promise by means of deceit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah quotes Isaac almost exactly, and adds, 'before Yahweh before my death.' Even in the midst of her plotting, she appeals to the solemnity of blessing before the Lord. It is a warning to us all: we can speak of God even while we are set on doing wrong in our own way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah urges Jacob to obey her voice in this matter. A mother's voice should guide to righteousness, but here it leads down a crooked path. I pray for all who have influence - that our words would point others to trust God's timing, not to seize His gifts by sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah sends Jacob for two young goats to be made into savory food. The plan is precise, deliberate, and deceitful. How different from our Savior, who could have seized power by force, yet chose to take upon Himself our shame to bring us blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob is to bring the food so that Isaac may bless him before his death. The goal is the blessing itself - which God had already promised - but the method is faithless and fraught with cost. God will indeed accomplish what He said, but Jacob will spend years reaping the fruit of this day's deception.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob objects not to the sin, but to the risk of being found out. His fear is of exposure and a curse, not of grieving his father or dishonoring the Lord. I know that kind of fear too - concerned more with getting caught than with doing what is right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob says he would bring a curse on himself, and not a blessing. How tragically ironic - he is worried about a curse from his blind father, yet he is about to bring grief to the whole house and a lifetime of fear upon himself. The only real blessing is from the Lord, not stolen by deceit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah tells Jacob to let the curse fall on her. A mother's love has gone terribly wrong here - willing to bear the consequence to get what she wants. No one should have to bear another's chosen sin, and yet our true Mother-Figure's son bore all our curses for us, willingly, so we might receive blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob goes and does it, and Rebekah makes savory food just as Isaac loved. The plan proceeds smoothly, which only makes the tragedy deeper. Sin often looks easy in the moment, but the Lord sees it all, and its harvest comes in due time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau's best clothes. Outwardly, he is made to look like the brother he is not. How like us - we try to cover ourselves with anything but the righteousness of Christ. Only God can clothe us in what truly makes us pleasing to the Father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The skins of young goats go on Jacob's hands and neck to mimic Esau's hairiness. Every detail is covered with deception. I grieve that we would rather disguise ourselves than be known as sinners who need mercy. But the God who knows us fully still loves to cover us fully in Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah puts the food into Jacob's hands. A mother who once carried him now sends him out to lie to his own father. Familial love has been twisted into something destructive. May the Lord heal our loves and root them first and foremost in love for Him and truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob comes to his father saying, 'My father?' Isaac answers, 'Here I am. Who are you, my son?' That question hangs heavy over the whole scene. The blind father asks to know his son, but the deceiving son is about to answer with a lie. How different from the day when our heavenly Father will fully know and fully receive all those who are in His true Son.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob says, 'I am Esau your firstborn.' With his mouth he takes the name and the birthright and the blessing. Three times in quick succession he speaks deceit. I tremble at how easily our tongues sin when our hearts are set on getting our way. Thank God for Jesus, who is ever truthful for us and speaks only truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac is astonished at how quickly the venison was found, and Jacob blasphemously attributes it to 'Yahweh your God.' He drags the holy name of the covenant God into his deception. How grievous to use the name we love to cover the sin we commit. The Lord will not hold such things guiltless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac wants to feel Jacob to be sure. The sense of touch will test what the ears have heard. God often uses circumstances to expose what is hidden, though here Isaac is still in the dark. There is coming a day when nothing will be hidden, and all will be revealed before our righteous Judge - yet for those in Christ, all is already covered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac discerns confusion - the voice is Jacob's, but the hands are Esau's. He wavers between doubt and desire to bless. Our hearts are so easily divided when we love what we should not and want what God has not purposed. How thankful I am that God's purposes are never swayed by our wavering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac does not recognize Jacob because of the hairy hands, and so he blesses him. The blessing goes out, irrevocable in form, though obtained by deceit. God's sovereign plan is moving forward even through the sins of His people. He will use Jacob, yet He will also lovingly discipline him for these very deeds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac asks again, point blank, 'Are you really my son Esau?' Jacob lies once more: 'I am.' There comes a point where one lie demands another, and the web grows tighter with every word. Thank God that our hope is not in being truthful enough, but in the One who is the Truth for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac eats and drinks, saying he will eat his son's venison that his soul may bless him. There is such sadness here - a father unwittingly blessing the son he did not intend to bless, while the son he loves is about to be brokenhearted. Sin always brings sorrow to those we love most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac asks Jacob to come near and kiss him. A final act of fatherly affection before the blessing. How tender, and how tragic that this kiss is received under false pretenses. Our Lord knew the kiss of betrayal, yet He went willingly to the cross to give true kisses of forgiveness to all who turn to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As Isaac smells Esau's clothes, he blesses Jacob with words that echo the blessing of Noah over Shem in Genesis 9:27 and look forward to God's covenant promises. He speaks of fields blessed by Yahweh and abundance of grain and new wine. Little does he know he is pronouncing the very blessing God had ordained, though through crooked means. God's Word always accomplishes what He purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac prays for dew from heaven and fatness of the earth, for plenty of grain and new wine. These are covenant blessings tied to the land God would give. For those in Jesus, our blessing is far greater - not merely rain and grain, but every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, secured for us forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peoples will serve Jacob and nations bow down to him; his brothers will bow to him. Isaac invokes curses on those who curse Jacob and blessings on those who bless him. This is strikingly close to God's words to Abraham in Genesis 12:3. God is confirming the covenant through this blessing, even if the vessel is flawed and the means are stained with sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No sooner has Jacob gone out than Esau comes in from hunting. The timing could not be more cruel. Two brothers, both longing for their father's blessing, cross paths in the doorway at the exact moment of heartbreak. Sin has made brothers enemies when God meant them to love one another.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau also brings savory food and asks his father to arise and eat, so that he may bless him. He does everything his father asked, just as he was told. Yet the blessing is already gone. Obedience at the right moment means nothing when the deed of faithlessness has already been done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac asks, 'Who are you?' and Esau replies, 'I am your son, your firstborn, Esau.' The same question as before, but now with a very different answer. Reality comes crashing in all at once for Isaac. How often we are blind until the moment of loss makes us see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac trembles violently and says, 'Who, then, is he... and I have blessed him? Yes, he will be blessed.' He recognizes the hand of God in it, even though he had been tricked. There is faith here - he submits to what God has done, knowing the blessing once spoken cannot be taken back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau cries with an exceeding great and bitter cry, begging for his father to bless him too. The sound of a broken heart. I grieve with him, yet I know that God gives us warnings and we often despise them until it is too late. How much more should we run to the One who still gives grace today while it may be found.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac tells Esau plainly that Jacob came with deceit and took away his blessing. The truth comes out at last, too late to undo it. Hidden sin always comes to light, and what we tried to gain by covertness brings public grief. God is just, and He is also faithful to keep His word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau says Jacob has rightly been named 'Heel-Catcher' - he has supplanted him twice, taking birthright and blessing. He laments that there is no blessing left for him. Hebrews 12:16-17 warns us not to be like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright and later found no place for repentance though he sought it with tears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac says he has already made Jacob lord over Esau and given him servants. He has sustained him with grain and new wine. With sorrow he asks what he can do for Esau. The father who wanted to bless his firstborn must now tell him there is little left. Our choices have consequences, though God's mercy is never exhausted for those who truly turn to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau asks, 'Have you but one blessing, my father?' and weeps loudly. He is grieved, but is he grieved over his sin or only over losing the blessing? The difference matters. Godly sorrow leads to repentance; worldly sorrow leads to death. I pray for a heart that grieves most of all over grieving my Savior.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaac blesses Esau, but differently - away from the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven. His dwelling will be of the land's richness, but not the same preeminence. God is just in giving to each what is fitting. Yet even here, there is no utter abandonment; Esau will have provision, just not the covenant headship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau will live by his sword and serve his brother, but the time will come when he will break loose and shake off Jacob's yoke. This prophecy would be fulfilled in later history as Edom rose against Israel. God's word stands, even when spoken in grief. He ordains the end of all things, and He is faithful to every word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Esau hates Jacob and plots murder in his heart. The days of mourning for his father give him cover for his evil plan. Hatred, like sin, grows in secret until it bursts forth in violence. The Lord sees the heart, and He will judge righteously. Yet our great Savior loves even His enemies and prays for those who would kill Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah hears of Esau's plan and acts quickly to protect Jacob. For all her earlier scheming, here she shows motherly care to save her son from death. God uses even flawed people to preserve the line through which the Savior would come. His faithfulness does not depend on ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah tells Jacob to flee to Laban in Haran. The blessing he stole has become a curse of fear, forcing him from home. He will go from being the one who grasped to being the one grasped at. God is merciful to discipline His children, leading them back to trust Him alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah says stay for a few days until Esau's fury turns away. Little does she know Jacob will be gone for twenty years, and she will never see him again. Sin's consequences always reach farther than we imagine. We sow in secret, but we reap in tears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah asks, 'Why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?' She fears losing both sons - Jacob to murder, Esau to the bloodguilt of killing his brother. The family she tried to unite by deceit is now on the brink of being torn apart forever. God is faithful to heal what our sin has broken, but He often does it through long and painful roads.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rebekah complains to Isaac about the daughters of Heth, using this as her reason to send Jacob away. It is a crafty appeal, but God uses it to accomplish what He had already planned. Readers today hear an echo of how the Lord takes our crooked schemes and weaves them into His perfect plan of redemption. As of 2026-10, I am grateful that His purposes cannot be thwarted, even by our sins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
